finding.headline: You plan to retire at 62, but Medicare starts at 65, so you would need other coverage for about 3 years.
details: Medicare generally starts when you turn 65, and the sign-up window runs for 7 months, starting 3 months before you turn 65. Signing up late can lead to a monthly late enrollment penalty that grows the longer you wait.
Social Security can start as early as 62, but full benefits apply only at full retirement age. Each month you delay past full retirement age raises your benefit, and the increase stops at 70.
For 2027, the 401(k) limit is $25,500 and the IRA limit is $7,500. Once you reach 50, the catch-up limit rises to $8,500 in 2027, so a 401(k) can reach $34,000 a year.

finding.headline: About 22% of your income goes to tax now, and about 10% of withdrawals in retirement.
details: Now, total tax is $68,667 of $310,000 pay. In retirement, tax is about $7,156 a year on withdrawals of $47,715.
Draw on taxable savings and cash first, then pre-tax accounts like your 401(k), and Roth accounts last. Pre-tax savings are 57% of your total, so they will carry most of your later tax.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Please check the order with a tax professional before you act.

finding.headline: You can count on $111,600 a year: $44,500 for basics and $67,100 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $44,500 a year.
Your spending goal is $105,000 a year, and the plan supports it in 94 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $90,634 a year: $23,000 into a 401(k) or IRA, $9,300 from your employer's match, $58,334 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Your spending in retirement leaves out the mortgage. The payments left after you retire, until 2046, are counted as a cost of their own.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $62,000 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70 for each of you, which pays about $76,900 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $51,300 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay and the child tax credit applies. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high. Your state taxes part of it too.
The plan runs to age 98. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
